# Water Quality Statistics

## Overview

We developed a set of inferential statistical models to estimate
chemical concentrations in stormwater runoff across the Puget Sound
watershed. Models were developed using spatial and temporal landscape
predictors for a subset of constituents of concern (COCs). These models
represent an advancement over current practices, which rely on
categorical land use designations (e.g., high vs. low density
residential, commercial, industrial) to approximate chemical
concentrations in stormwater. While this method is convenient, it has
some limitations. In particular, categorical land use designations vary
by jurisdiction, limiting applicability of results between jurisdictions
over a landscape. A qualitative comparison of existing land cover data
sources and self-reported land use types revealed little agreement among
jurisdictions' definitions of land use categories. We therefore
hypothesized that land use designation alone would be a poor predictor
of chemical concentration in unmonitored basins.

Therefore, our objectives were to:

1.  Find a stronger, more data-driven method of predicting chemical
    concentration compared to the current method of using categorical
    land use designations to assign concentrations. Here, we investigate
    the potential for using continuous, measurable landscape spatial
    predictors (also referred to as **spatial predictors**) that can be
    objectively measured across large regions, thereby increasing the
    applicability of model results across jurisdictional boundaries. 
2.  Determine whether a landscape spatial predictor approach produces
    stronger predictive power than either a null model or the current
    categorical land use model.

In order to achieve these objectives, we developed null, categorical
land use, and landscape spatial predictor models to estimate
concentrations for constituents of concern in Puget Sound stormwater. We
define these models in the following way (details provided later):

1.  **Null Model:** COC concentration is equal to median COC
    concentration over all sampling dates and locations.
2.  **Categorical Land Use Model:** COC concentration is modeled as a
    linear mixed effects model, utilizing land use category (high
    density residential [HDR], low density residential [LDR], commercial
    [COM], industrial [IND]), precipitation (rainfall and/or antecedent
    dry days) and season (for COCs where a seasonal trend appeared in
    the data).
3.  **Spatial Predictor Model:** COC concentration is modeled as a
    linear mixed effects model, utilizing up to three landscape spatial
    predictors, precipitation (rainfall and/or antecedent dry days) and
    season (for COCs where a seasonal trend appeared in the data).

Landscape spatial predictors were drawn from various spatial data layers
(e.g., traffic, forest cover, impervious surface cover), spatio-temporal
layers (e.g., rainfall and seasonality), as well as land use
(commercial, industrial, residential). These models were then compared
against the null and categorical land use models for model fit and
predictive ability. The best fit models were translated to the
Stormwater Heatmap online communication tool using colors to show
predicted pollutant concentration. For all COCs analyzed, the spatial
predictor model out-performed the null model and the categorical land
use model.

In addition to COC concentration estimates, the Stormwater Heatmap also
provides stormwater managers with an understanding of the underlying
variability in estimated COC concentrations presented on the Stormwater
Heatmap. We achieved this on a sub-basin scale by calculating Bayesian
80% confidence intervals (known as credible intervals) for each
sub-basin. This information can be accessed in the Stormwater Heatmap by
choosing a geospatial sub-basin dataset to aggregate results (HUC12:
USGS Watershed Boundary dataset; Washington Department of Ecology Puget
Sound Assessment Units; or NHDPlus high resolution watershed dataset),
and clicking on a sub-basin to view a pop-up window indicating the 80%
upper and lower credible intervals for that sub-basin.

## Data Sources

### Outfall Data

The primary source of observed stormwater data is the S8.D Municipal
Stormwater Permit Outfall Data (referred to as the S8 Data in this
document) provided by the Washington Department of Ecology (Hobbs et
al., 2015). Special Condition S8.D of the 2007-2012 Phase I Municipal
Stormwater Permit required permittees to collect and analyze data to
evaluate chemical concentrations in stormwater discharged from
catchments with the following self-reported land uses: High Density
Residential (HDR), Low Density Residential (LDR), Commercial (COM) and
Industrial (IND). Phase I Permittees[^1] measured water quality,
discharge, and other parameters from stormwater outfalls during storm
events. Stormwater data collected from a total of 14 catchments by six
Phase I Permittees were utilized in this modeling study.

[^1]: Phase I Permittees include: cities of Tacoma and Seattle; King,
    Snohomish, Pierce and Clark counties; Ports of Tacoma and Seattle. 
    For this study, all data were used with the exception of those from
    Clark County (outside of the Puget Sound region) and Port of Seattle
    (too different from all other Puget Sound watersheds).

The S8 Data are available from the Washington Department of Ecology
(hereafter referred to as Ecology) via an open-data api at:
[https://data.wa.gov/Natural-Resources-Environment/Municipal-Stormwater-
Permit-Outfall-Data/d958-q2ci.](https://data.wa.gov/Natural-Resources-Environment/Municipal-Stormwater-%20Permit-Outfall-Data/d958-q2ci.%20)

COCs analyzed in this study are:

- Total Copper

- Total Suspended Solids (TSS)

- Total Phosphorus

- Total Zinc

- Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN)

We extracted data for these COCs, and performed minimal data cleaning.
We filtered out rejected data (values with a R or REJ flag), removed
replicates, and removed one data point for TKN that was an outlier (an
order of magnitude higher than the majority of the data). Figure 4.1
shows data before removal of the outlier.

![](images/COC%20all%20data%20with%20outliers%20Fig%204_1.bmp)

**Figure 4.1** All observations with outlier in place for Total Kjeldahl
nitrogen (TKN)

### Censored (Non-Detect) Data

Nearly all COCs had non-detect (ND; left-censored) data present (Table
4.1). Ecology flagged non-detect data and provided the reporting limit
for each non-detect value. The EPA allows substitution of (0.5 x
detection limit) for censored values when less than 15% of samples are
non-detect (USEPA, 2009). However, substitution can add a pattern to the
data that is different than the pattern of the data itself, with the
likelihood increasing as the proportion of non-detect data increases
(Helsel, 2012). In the S8 Data, most COCs had only a small percentage of
data that were non-detect (\<1.2%); for these, non-detect values were
substituted with one-half of the reporting limit, which is allowed by
EPA guidelines, providing less than 15% of samples are non-detect
(USEPA, 2009). TKN had a higher level of non-detect data (approximately
10%). We decided not to perform substitution of non-detect TKN samples
to avoid introducing a pattern to the data that is different than the
data itself (Helsel 2012). Instead, regression on order statistics (ROS)
was employed to calculate statistics for TKN. (See the Total Kjeldahl
Nitrogen section under the Results heading for details.)

**Table 4.1** Percentage of data points that were non-detect
(left-censored) for each COC. ND: Non-detect.

![](images/Table%204_1.bmp)

### Transformation of outfall data

Each COC was evaluated for its underlying distribution, to determine
whether transformation would be beneficial prior to analysis.
Quantile-quantile plots (QQ plots) using a normal distribution, gamma
distribution, square-root transformed distribution, and log-transformed
distribution were visually analyzed. For all COC's, log-transformation
was deemed an appropriate data transformation prior to model analysis
(Fig. 4.2).

![](images/QQ%20plots%20all%20COCs%20fig%204_2.bmp)

**Figure 4.2** Quantile-quantile plots of COCs using a natural-log (ln)
scale. Red line shows the QQ-line.

## Landscape Spatial Data

For this study, we did not rely on the permittee's self-reported land
use type. As described earlier, a qualitative comparison of existing
land cover data sources and self-reported land use types revealed little
agreement among permittee definitions of the four land use types (HDR,
LDR, COM, IND). Furthermore, areas with mixed land use types (e.g.: 30%
commercial, 40% high density residential) could only correspond to one
land use type. Therefore, we compiled a suite of continuous datasets for
use in fitting and comparing models that estimate chemical
concentration. We divide the datasets into two groups: continuous land
use data and landscape data.

### Continuous Land Use Data

In order to employ a consistent analysis across different monitored
watersheds we extracted land use data from the Washington Department of
Commerce: Puget Sound Mapping Project
(<https://www.commerce.wa.gov/serving-communities/growth-management/puget-sound-mapping-project>).
Land use classes (also listed in Table 4.2) include:

- Intensive urban (includes commercial areas, apartment buildings)

- Urban residential (includes the majority of urban and suburban
  single-family dwellings)

- Rural residential

- Industrial

In addition, we combined some land use classes to generate additional
land use classes:

- Total residential (urban residential + rural residential)

- Intensive Urban + Industrial (the industrial land use category only
  had a few non-zero data points)

### Landscape Data

For each watershed contained in the S8 Data, potentially relevant
landscape data and their source are provided in Table 4.2. Additionally,
several data sets were derived from these sources, including:

- totRES and intURB_IND — each of these are a grouping of similar land
  use categories (urban + rural residential; intensive urban +
  industrial) from the Washington State Department of Commerce: Puget
  Sound Mapping Project. Combining categories allowed us to combine some
  less common land uses from the S8 dataset (rural residential;
  industrial) with similar, more common land uses (urban residential;
  intensive urban);

- roof_urbRES, roof_totRES and roof_intURB -- derived from rooftop
  density (Robertson et al, in prep) applied to land use data
  (Washington State Department of Commerce: Puget Sound Mapping
  Project);

- greenery — sum of low vegetation/grass, medium vegetation/shrub, and
  trees (Robertson et al, in prep);

- greeneryBE — sum of low vegetation/grass, medium vegetation/shrub,
  trees, and bare earth (e.g., exposed rock, mud flats, unvegetated
  fields); data from Robertson et al, in prep;

- not_greenBE — greeneryBE subtracted from 1, to yield the proportion of
  land cover that is not greenery or bare earth; data from Robertson et
  al, in prep;

- CO2_transport -- sum of road, rail and commercial marine vessel CO2
  data from Gurney et al., 2019;

- CO2_almostTotal -- sum of commercial, residential, road, nonroad, rail
  and commercial marine vessel CO2 data from Gurney et al., 2019;

- devAge - calculated based on proportion of land developed by year
  range, using Pesaresi et al., 2005 data in the following equation:
  devAge = 4\*dev_pre_1975 + 3\*dev_1975_1990 + 2\*dev_1990_2000 +
  1\*dev_2000_2014. Values close to 0 indicate little to no development,
  while values close to 4 indicate high or old development.

**Table 4.2** Sources of landscape spatial predictor data used to
develop statistical models.

![](images/Table%204_2-02.bmp)

### Pre-processing of spatial data

In order to use the landscape spatial data at an appropriate scale
across the study area, spatial predictors were stacked and then
convolved with a 100-meter gaussian kernel. This resulted in "fuzzy"
predictors that could apply across dataset boundaries. These values were
then extracted for each monitored watershed.

### Transformation

For some spatial data, the presence of outliers indicated that
transformation would be beneficial. Spatial data were scaled and
centered, then plotted and visually assessed for outliers (Fig. 4.3).

![](images/untransformed%20standardized%20predictors%20tall.bmp)**Figure
4.3** Untransformed, standardized spatial data. Standardization was
performed by subtracting the mean of the 14 catchments, and dividing by
the standard deviation.

Square-root transformation was performed on spatial data sets with
outliers that were higher than the rest of the predictor's values,
including: slope, popn, CO2_almostTotal, CO2_com, CO2_nonroad, CO2_res,
CO2_road, and CO2_transport. The devAge spatial predictor had a low data
outlier; devAge values were squared to address the low outlier
(devAge\^2).

Additionally, traffic was square-root transformed. We decided on a
square-root transformation for traffic for several reasons. 1.) From
highway runoff data, we observed that heavy metal concentrations do not
increase uniformly as traffic increases; rather, the slope looks as if
it should be steeper at first, then gradually less steep at higher
traffic levels (see Fig. 4 in Kayhanian et al., 2003; see also Fig. 3-1
in CalTrans 2003). This indicates that a weaker transformation for the
traffic predictor (e.g., square-root transformation) would be a good
choice in conjunction with the stronger transformation
(ln-transformation) that was needed for COCs (dependent variable). 2.)
The catchments represented by the S8 Data have traffic values up to
20,000 AADT. However, the mapped Stormwater Heatmap domain has traffic
levels up to 160,000. Square-root transformation of the traffic
predictor leads to a more linear pattern in credible interval ranges as
traffic levels increase, while the untransformed traffic predictor has a
more exponential pattern in credible interval ranges at higher traffic
levels. Considering patterns in the highway runoff data, we decided that
the square-root transformation would be appropriate for traffic.

Figure 4.4 shows the spatial data following transformation. Prior to use
in models, spatial data sets were scaled and centered using the mean and
standard deviation from the 14 catchments in this study.

![](images/transformed%20standardized%20predictors-02.bmp)**Figure 4.4**
Spatial data following transformation and standardization.

### Precipitation Data

Daily rainfall data were obtained from the Daymet website operated by
NASA (<https://daymet.ornl.gov/>; Thornton et al 2022). Daily data were
obtained for years 2009 to 2013, and cumulative one-day, three-day,
seven-day, 14-day, 21-day and 28-day antecedent precipitation was
calculated for each sampling date. For example, for a sampling date of
March 24, cumulative three-day precipitation would include precipitation
occurring on March 22, 23 and 24. For each COC, *ln*-transformed COC
concentrations were plotted against each precipitation measurement, and
the plots were visually assessed to select the most appropriate time
scale for precipitation. Cumulative 21-day precipitation was selected
for copper and phosphorus, cumulative 14-day precipitation was selected
for zinc and TKN, and cumulative 1-day precipitation was selected for
TSS.

## Model Construction and Selection

The structure of the data, with multiple data points over time for each
of the 14 catchments, indicated that mixed effects models would be
appropriate. We considered both a frequentist statistical framework, as
well as a Bayesian framework for running the mixed effects models, and
ended up utilizing a combination of the two. The frequentist framework
is significantly faster to perform, and was used to identify the best
set of spatial predictors as fixed effects, as well as to identify the
best variance structure (see Steps 1-7, below).

Once the best fit model was selected, we fit the same model in a
Bayesian framework; this allowed us to compute credible intervals around
estimated COC values. Frequentist statistical methods are not able to
properly estimate variability around random effects, so Bayesian methods
were needed for this step.

Within a frequentist statistical framework, selection of the best model
for each COC was performed using the methodology of Zuur et al. (2009),
as outlined in Steps 1-7 below. Statistical analyses and model fitting
were performed in R (R Core Team, 2021). Following the frequentist
analysis, we moved into a Bayesian framework for Steps 8-9, which
included model examination and credible interval calculations.

### Step 1. Select strong potential spatial predictors

The initial step was to find a suitable set of potential spatial
predictors for each of the COCs evaluated. Single-predictor linear
models were constructed for the relationship between *ln*-transformed
chemical concentration and each spatial predictor, in turn. Plots were
visually assessed to determine candidate predictors for linear mixed
effects models. We looked for slopes with a p-value of \< 0.05, and for
data points to fall roughly along the best fit model line.

### Step 2. Construct a beyond-optimal model, controlling for collinearity

The starting point of our model selection process was a "beyond-optimal"
model, where the fixed component of the mixed effects model contained as
many strong spatial predictors as possible, as well as weather-based
spatio-temporal predictors with potential importance (cumulative
precipitation, season, antecedant dry days):

$$ln(C)_{ijk} = fixed.effects_{ijk} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

Where:

*C* = concentration of chemical

*i* = sample

*j* = monitored catchment (location)

*k* = reporting agency, and

$\epsilon_{ijk}$ = unexplained error

To prevent using highly correlated spatial predictors together in the
beyond-optimal model, we calculated the correlation coefficient for each
pair of spatial predictors and eliminated select predictors to reduce
correlation. We then constructed a generalized least squares (gls) model
in R (nlme package, Pinheiro et al., 2021) using the beyond-optimal set
of fixed effects and utilizing restricted maximum likelihood estimation
(REML).

Throughout the model selection process, highly correlated spatial
predictors (correlation coefficient ≥0.85) were not used together in any
models.

### Step 3. Control for heterogeneity (heteroskedasticity)

Normalized residuals from the beyond-optimal gls model were plotted
against the model's fitted values and examined for heteroskedasticity.
We also plotted residuals against reporting agency, year, season, land
use, cumulative precipitation, antecedent dry days, and all potential
spatial predictors, to look for patterns in residuals. If residual plots
showed evidence of heteroskedasticity, we tried a series of gls models
(fitted with REML) with different variance structures that utilized
reporting agency, location, season, and precipitation as variance
covariates. Variance structure for each COC was selected based on the
lowest Akaike information criterion (AIC) and Bayesian information
criterion (BIC) scores.

If no heteroskedasticity was present, residuals were assumed to be
normally distributed, with mean 0 and standard deviation $$\sigma$$

$$\epsilon_{ijk} \sim N(0, \sigma) $$

Controlling for heteroskedasticity often involved allowing each location
*j* or each reporting agency *k* to have a different standard deviation,
such that:

$$sd(\epsilon_{ijk})=\sigma_j; \quad\text{  }\quad \epsilon_{ijk} \sim N(0, \sigma_j)$$

or

$$sd(\epsilon_{ijk})=\sigma_k; \quad\text{  }\quad \epsilon_{ijk} \sim N(0, \sigma_k)$$

### Step 4. Find the proper random effects structure

Next, we used the beyond-optimal model with the correct variance
structure to find the proper random effects structure. In the case of
our data set, we had six sampling agencies, each with 1 to 3 locations,
and multiple samples collected over time at each location. The nested
structure of our data, along with our interest in using the model to
predict results in locations that haven't been sampled (rather than to
compare sampled locations and agencies to each other), led to the
identification of *reporting* *agency* and *location* as potential
nested random effects. In this situation, the random part of a nested
mixed effects model has the form:

$$random.effects_{ijk} = a_k + a_{j|k} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

where $a_k$ is a random intercept that allows for variation between
agencies, while $a_{j|k}$ represents variation between locations (*j*)
from the same reporting agency (*k*). We assumed that $a_k$ and
$a_{j|k}$ are normally distributed, with standard deviations given
below:

$$a_k \sim N(0, \sigma_{agency})$$

$$a_{j|k}\sim N(0, \sigma_{location})$$

The beyond-optimal gls model was compared to a linear mixed effects
(lme) nested random-intercept model (nlme package, Pinheiro et al.,
2021) fitted with REML, where the intercept was allowed to change per
agency, and per location nested within reporting agency. Because the gls
model and the random-intercept model are nested models, they were
compared using a likelihood ratio test to see if one model was
significantly better than the other (p-value \< 0.05). The best-fit
model was then selected based on the lowest AIC value. For all COCs, the
nested random-intercept model fit the data better than the gls model
with no random effects.

Intuitively, a random intercept for location nested within reporting
agency is suitable for the stormwater data. Each location was sampled
multiple times over the 4-year data collection period, and we would
expect data within a location to be more similar than data between two
locations. Additionally, reporting agencies may have differed slightly
in sample collection methodologies, including: timing of sample
collection once a storm began, selection of laboratory for sample
analysis, and any biases in selection of representative catchments.
These differences could lead to variability in COC results by reporting
agency, and can be neatly captured in the random component of the model.

### Step 5. Check for temporal and spatial correlation

The beyond-optimal model with the correct variance structure and random
effects structure was then examined for evidence of temporal and spatial
auto-correlation. Temporal auto-correlation plots were generated and
visually assessed for indications of correlation between various
sampling time lags; no evidence of temporal autocorrelation was found
for any COC. Spatial auto-correlation was assessed through two methods:
variograms, and spatially-explicit bubble plots of model residuals; no
compelling indications of spatial autocorrelation was found for any COC.

All tests for temporal and spatial auto-correlation were repeated
following selection of best-fit models.

### Step 6. Find the proper fixed effects structure

We used the strong potential spatial predictors from Step 1 to generate
an exhaustive set of fixed-effects formulae with combinations of one,
two and three spatial predictors. Predictors with high correlation
coefficients (≥0.85) were not placed into formulae together.

A set of models was generated using the fixed effects formulae, along
with the best-fit random effects and variance structures identified in
steps 3 and 4. Linear mixed effects models were applied using the nlme
package (Pinheiro et al, 2021), and fitting with maximum likelihood (ML)
estimation[^2]. Models where the sign (+ or --) of the spatial predictor
coefficients did not match the coefficient signs from the linear model
from Step 1 were discarded. Models were then sorted according to AIC
value, and the top 20 models were examined for fit to individual
predictors. If weak spatial or spatio-temporal predictors (p-value \>
0.05) were present in the model, these were eliminated, then plots of
residuals versus fitted values, reporting agency, location, and spatial
predictors were examined. One to three candidate models were selected
for consideration as the best spatial predictor model. Selection
priority was given to simpler models to prevent over-fitting. In
situations where models with one or two spatial predictors performed
slightly worse than the best models with three spatial predictors, the
models with less predictors were selected.

[^2]: As described in Faraway (2006), pg 156, REML estimation should not
    be used to compare models with different fixed effects because REML
    estimates the random effects by considering linear combinations of
    the data that remove the fixed effects. If the fixed effects change,
    the likelihoods of the two models will not be directly comparable.
    However, REML is generally considered to give better estimates for
    the random effects, so final models were fitted with REML

Candidate models all had low AIC values, acceptable residual plots, and
good fit to individual spatial predictors. The form of the candidate
models was:

$$ln(C)_{ijk}=fixed.effects_{ijk} + a_k + a_{j|k} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

Using knowledge of chemical contaminant sources and mobilization into
stormwater, we selected the best spatial predictor model for each COC.

### Step 7. Final model comparison to categorical land use models

Three models were ultimately fitted with REML and compared for each COC.
This allowed us to assess the suitability of models built with spatial
predictors, and ultimately to determine whether COC approximations made
with spatial landscape predictors offer an improvement over those made
with categorical land use designations. The three models for each COC
include:

1.  **Null Model:** COC concentration is equal to median COC
    concentration over all sampling dates and locations

2.  **Categorical Land Use Model:** COC concentration is modeled as a
    linear mixed effects model, utilizing land use category (HDR, LDR,
    COM, IND), precipitation (rainfall and/or antecedent dry days), and
    season (for COCs where a seasonal trend appeared in the data).

3.  **Spatial Predictor Model:** COC concentration is modeled as a
    linear mixed effects model, utilizing up to three spatial
    predictors, precipitation (rainfall and/or antecedent dry days), and
    season (for COCs where a seasonal trend appeared in the data).

We compared these three models using AIC, to determine which model had
the best fit to data. For all COCs analyzed, the spatial predictor model
out-performed the null model and the categorical land use model; thus,
the spatial predictor model for each COC was pushed forward for Bayesian
model analysis. In the case of total phosphorus, an even simpler model
including only rainfall and seasonal components had a slight improvement
over the spatial predictor model in the frequentist framework, so both
models were pushed forward for Bayesian model analysis.

Bayesian models were expected to yield similar parameter values to the
frequentist models. As previously mentioned, Bayesian analysis allows
computation of confidence intervals (called credible intervals in
Bayesian statistics) around estimated COC values when random effects are
present. Frequentist mixed effects models are not capable of accurately
estimating variability around random effects, so confidence intervals
calculated using frequentist statistics underestimate the uncertainty
around each COC estimate. As discussed in Step 6, given the structure of
the S8 Data (repeat sampling over time at catchment locations), along
with methodological differences in stormwater sampling that could
introduce variability in COC values across agencies, we felt it critical
to include random effects and their associated variability in the models
and their precision estimates.

### Step 8. Bayesian model analysis

The best fit frequentist model structure from Step 7 (made up of the
variance structure from Step 3, random effects structure from Step 4,
and fixed effects structure from Step 6) was then applied to a Bayesian
framework using the brms package in R (Buerkner, 2017). The brms package
provides an R interface for performing Bayesian multi-level (mixed
effects) regression models using the programming language Stan in the
background (Stan Development Team, 2022).

The brms algorithm accepts a prior distribution for each parameter (we
assumed an uninformative prior distribution for each spatial predictor:
Normal distribution with mean = 0 and standard deviation = 10) and
provides an output of 4000 sets of parameter estimates that collectively
make up what is called the posterior. The parameter sets vary in their
likelihood given the data, and the parameter set with the highest
likelihood is used in the Stormwater Heatmap.

Models were examined for the following elements:

1.  [model convergence]{.underline} and adequate sampling of the
    parameter space using posterior traces. These address the questions:
    did the model look at enough parameter values? Was it able to find a
    best fit model using the given predictors?

2.  [appropriateness of the variance structure]{.underline}. For some
    COCs, the difference in AIC value between models using location vs.
    reporting agency as a variance covariate was small. In these cases,
    the best-fit fixed effects and random effects structures were
    applied to models with different variance structures. The resulting
    models were compared using the leave-one-out information criterion
    (LOOIC - similar to AIC, where lower values indicate better model
    fit) to identify the best variance structure.

3.  [model diagnostics]{.underline} using leave-one-out cross-validation
    (LOOCV) to calculate the Pareto *k* shape parameter. The Pareto *k*
    shape parameter provides an assessment of reliability and
    convergence rate of the Bayesian model estimator: a Pareto *k* value
    is calculated for each data point, and influential outliers that may
    reduce the model's reliability are identified by Pareto *k* values
    \> 0.7. When we identified models with Pareto *k* values above 0.7,
    we fitted Bayesian models using an underlying Student-t distribution
    rather than the default Gaussian distribution, to see if this
    resolved the issue. The Student-t distribution has thicker tails,
    which can encompass some more extreme observations. Models utilizing
    the Student-t distribution include an extra parameter, $\nu$, for
    describing the shape of the Student-t distribution; this extra
    parameter was estimated by the Bayesian model in cases where a model
    using the Student-t distribution provided the best fit.

4.  [graphical posterior predictive checking]{.underline}. We generated
    density plots of observed data along with simulated values from the
    posterior predictive distribution, to ensure that model-generated
    COC estimates fit observed data. We also examined observed vs.
    estimated plots. Graphical posterior predictive checking addresses
    the questions: Did the model correctly approximate the posterior
    distribution? Knowing that models are useful fiction and always fail
    in some way, how does *our* model fail?

5.  [calculate model precision]{.underline} using root mean square error
    (RMSE) and RMSE-observations standard deviation ratio (RSR). RMSE
    was calculated by squaring residuals, finding the average of the
    squared residuals, then taking the square-root of that average. RSR
    is a standardized version of RMSE, calculated as RSR=RMSE/standard
    deviation of observations.

6.  [analysis of sensitivity and uncertainty]{.underline}. We examined
    three facets of sensitivity in the models:

    1.  Are there influential data points, and if so, are the model
        conclusions sensitive to those influential data points?

    2.  Does changing the variance structure result in a quantitative
        change to the parameters for spatial landscape predictors?

    3.  If our selected random effects structure (samples nested within
        outfall locations nested within agencies) is incorrect, does a
        simpler structure (samples nested within outfall locations)
        result in qualitative differences to the model outcome?

The Bayesian model with the best variance structure and appropriate
underlying distribution (Gaussian or Student-t) was then used to
generate the heatmap layer, and to calculate credible intervals.

### Step 9. Obtain Credible Intervals from Bayesian model

Using the Bayesian model from Step 8, we calculated 80% credible
intervals (80% CIs; analogous to confidence intervals in frequentist
statistics) for all watershed sub-basins in the heatmap region. The
Stormwater Heatmap 80% CIs can be interpreted as follows: there is an
80% probability that the true (but unknown) mean COC concentration will
lie within the credible interval, given the evidence provided by the
observed data.  

Spatial means by sub-basin (called sub-basin reductions) were calculated
for spatial landscape predictors (e.g., traffic level, development age).
Three sub-basin reductions with different boundaries were used: Puget
Sound Assessment Units (PSAU), the USGS watershed boundary dataset
(HUC12), and the National Hydrography Dataset Plus (NHDPlus). 

Stormwater Heatmap credible intervals need to account for a variety of
realistic precipitation regimes and seasonal variation (e.g., wet vs.
dry season), because these factors are important predictors in most of
the COC models. We generated a set of realistic precipitation/season
regimes by randomly sampling 10% of the S8 Data (47 samples total) for
combined rain and season conditions. Forty-two of the samples were
randomly selected from non-summer months, and five samples were randomly
selected from summer months (July, August, September); this approximated
the split between wet and dry seasons in the S8 Data, where 11% of data
points were collected during summer months. Precipitation/season regimes
were combined with sub-basin reductions to generate a data frame where
each sub-basin was paired with each of the 47 options for
precipitation/season. We will refer to this data frame as SBR.PS
(sub-basin reduction/ precipitation, season). 

Credible intervals for each sub-basin reduction were calculated using
the fitted function (brms package; Buerkner, 2017) applied to the SBR.PS
data frame. The fitted function runs each entry in the SBR.PS data frame
through all 4000 parameter combinations generated in the Bayesian model,
producing 4000\*47 estimates of COC concentration in each sub-basin.
Credible interval estimates were grouped by sub-basin and summarized for
upper 80% CI and lower 80% CI. In this way, we were able to integrate
precipitation and season into the credible intervals. 

Stormwater Heatmap 80% credible intervals are provided for new,
unsampled locations, where the 80% interval corresponds to the mean COC
concentration at the new location, assuming that the new location is
sampled many times. The credible intervals account for two of the three
sources of model uncertainty: 

1.  uncertainty around the population-level intercept ($\beta_0$) and
    around the fixed effects parameters associated with spatial
    landscape predictors $\beta_3$ and $\beta_4$; and

2.  uncertainty around the variance parameters of the groups:
    $\sigma_{agency}$ and $\sigma_{location}$.

Residual (observation-level) variance, $\epsilon_{ijk}$, is not
accounted for in 80% CIs.

### Step 10. Translating Bayesian models to the Stormwater Heatmap

Bayesian model equations are substantially simplified for the Stormwater
Heatmap communication tool, which displays over-annual mean predicted
COC concentrations. Spatio-temporal predictors (rain, season) are set to
their mean value of 0, and the variance structure and nested random
effects terms are also set to their mean values of 0. Thus, the generic
COC equation:
$$\ln(C_{ijk}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1*rain_i + \beta_2*summer_i + \beta_3*predictor1_{ijk} + \beta_4*predictor2_{ijk} + a_k + a_{j|k} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

$$a_k \sim N(0, \sigma_{agency})$$

$$a_{j|k}\sim N(0, \sigma_{location})$$

$$\epsilon_{ijk} \sim N(0, \sigma_k)$$

simplifies to:

$$\ln(C) = \beta_0 + \beta_3*predictor1 + \beta_4*predictor2$$

for the Stormwater Heatmap. See the section **Translating Equations to
the Stormwater Heatmap** at the end of this chapter for more details.

## Results

Spatial predictor models provided the best fit to data for all COCs
analyzed, when compared with null models and categorical land use
models. Table 4.3 shows the spatial predictor model equations for
over-annual mean COC concentrations, which are displayed in the
pollutant layers of the Stormwater Heatmap. For most COCs, the full
spatial predictor models that were fitted to all data points also
include precipitation (rain) and season (summer/dry season vs. not
summer/wet season).

Detailed model-fitting results for each COC are provided in the sections
below.

over-annual mean concentrations of constituents of concern.

### Total Copper

Based on linear models of *ln*-transformed copper versus individual
spatial predictors, the strong spatial predictors identified for copper
include: totRES, intURB, intURB_IND, grass, greenery, impervious, nodev,
sqrt_traffic, sqrt_popn, pm25_na, sqrt_CO2_com, sqrt_CO2_road,
sqrt_CO2_nonroad, sqrt_CO2_almostTotal, sqrt_CO2_transport, devAge2, and
roof_intURB_IND (Fig 4.5).

![](images/Copper%20strong%20predictors.bmp)**Figure 4.5** Strong
spatial predictors for copper, showing linear model fit (blue line) for
the relationship between ln-transformed copper concentration and each
predictor in turn.

The precipitation predictor used for copper was 21-day cumulative
precipitation. In addition, evidence of higher copper concentrations
during summer led us to add *summer* as a categorical predictor to the
copper model, where *summer* = 1 during July, August, September, and
*summer* = 0 for all other months.

Residuals plotted against fitted values showed signs of slight
heterogeneity (Fig 4.6, top left). Of the variance structures tested,
the best fit allows residual variation to differ by location *j.*

$$sd(\epsilon_{ijk}) = \sigma_j$$

![](images/Copper%20variance%20structure%20plot.bmp)

**Figure 4.6** Normalized residuals from beyond-optimal model, with no
variance structure (top left), with reporting agency as a variance
covariate (top right), and with location as a variance covariate (bottom

#### Frequentist Model Summary

The best model for copper is a random-intercept model, where the
intercept of the linear model is allowed to vary by reporting agency
(*k*), and by location within each reporting agency (*j*\|*k*). No signs
of temporal or spatial auto-correlation were detected in
auto-correlation plots or variograms.

Two possible models emerged to capture the fixed effects:

$$ln(Cu_{ijk}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 * rain_i + \beta_2 * summer_i + \beta_3 * sqrt\_CO_2\_road_{ijk} + \beta_4 * devAge2_{ijk} + a_k + a_{j|k} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

$$ln(Cu_{ijk}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 * rain_i + \beta_2 * summer_i + \beta_3 * sqrt\_traffic_{ijk} + \beta_4 * devAge2_{ijk} + a_k + a_{j|k} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

The first model's AIC score was slightly lower than that of the second
model (AIC=699.3 vs. 700.9, when models were fitted with ML); however,
vehicle wear is more directly associated with copper in stormwater than
are emissions. As a result, we selected the second model, with
*sqrt_traffic* as a predictor. Figure 4.7 shows the model fit for each
individual predictor, plotted against data points. Correlation between
the two predictors was low (correlation = 0.3).

![](images/Copper%20single%20predictors%20plot.bmp)

**Figure 4.7** Single-predictor plots for copper, showing fit of the
Spatial Predictor Model to each predictor in turn. Model fitting was
performed using maximum likelihood (ML) estimation.

Comparisons between the Null Model, Categorical Land Use Model, and
Spatial Predictor Model can be visualized through residuals (Fig. 4.8)
and comparative metrics such as AIC. The residual plots clearly show
good fit (residuals close to zero) for the Categorical Land Use Model
and for the Spatial Predictor Model.

![](images/Copper%20residual%20plot%20for%203%20models.bmp)**Figure
4.8** Copper model residuals for the Null Model, Categorical Land Use
Model, and Spatial Predictor Model. Each bar represents one watershed,
with colors representing reporting agencies. Model fitting was performed
using maximum likelihood (ML) estimation.

Final frequentist model AIC values (fitted with REML) for the three
models are: 1317.1 (Null Model), 721.9 (Categorical Land Use Model) and
718.0 (Spatial Predictor Model), with the Spatial Predictor Model
showing an improvement over the Categorical Land Use Model. Final
coefficient values for all three frequentist models are shown in Figure
4.9. The large variability in model coefficients for the Categorical
Land Use Model (shown in blue) indicates lower predictive power of this
model. As a result, the Spatial Predictor model outperforms the
currently used Categorical Land Use-type model both in terms of AIC, as
well as in its potential for generating tighter precision intervals
around estimates of copper concentration. We selected this improved
method of estimating COC loading for inclusion in the Stormwater
Heatmap's data visualizations.

![](images/Copper%20model%20parameters.bmp)

**Figure 4.9** Frequentist model coefficients for the Null Model
(green), Categorical Land Use Model (blue), and Spatial Predictor Model
(red). These coefficient values for linear mixed effects models are
based on fitting with restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation,
and may differ slightly from those fitted using maximum likelihood (ML)
estimation.

#### Bayesian Model Summary

The Bayesian model for total copper follows a Student-t distribution
with the form:

$$\ln(Cu_{ijk}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1*rain_{i} + \beta_2*summer_{i} + \beta_3*sqrt\_traffic_{ijk} + \beta_4*devAge2_{ijk} + a_k + a_{j|k} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

where:

$$\beta_0 = 2.33;\quad\text{  }\quad \beta_1 = -0.18;\quad\text{  }\quad \beta_2=0.37;\quad\text{  }\quad \beta_3=0.43;\quad\text{  }\quad \beta_4=0.46$$

$$a_k \sim N(0, \sigma_{agency});\quad\text{  }\quad \sigma_{agency} = 0.21$$

$$a_{j|k}\sim N(0, \sigma_{location}); \quad\text{  }\quad \sigma_{location} = 0.45$$

$$\epsilon_{ijk} \sim t_{7.8}(0, \sigma_j); \quad\text{    }\quad ln(\sigma_j) = \eta + u_j; \quad\text{    }\quad \sigma_j = e^{\eta} * e^{u_j}; \quad\text{    }\quad \eta=-0.91; $$
$$ 
u_j \sim N(0,\sigma_0); \quad\text{    }\quad \sigma_0=0.21$$

Rain is 21-day cumulative precipitation, standardized; summer is a
factor with value = 1 for July, August, September, and value = 0 for all
other months. Both spatial predictors (traffic and development age) were
first transformed then standardized prior to use. Subscripts indicate
sample (*i*), location (*j*) and reporting agency (*k*).

Random effects $a_k$ (agency-specific contribution to the intercept) and
$a_{j|k}$ (location-specific contribution to the intercept) follow a
normal (Gaussian) distribution, with mean equal to 0 and standard
deviation equal to $\sigma_{agency}$ for agency-specific contribution to
the intercept, and $\sigma_{location}$ for location-specific
contribution to the intercept. The residual variance $\epsilon_{ijk}$
represents remaining variation in the data that cannot be explained by
the model variables. For the copper model, residual variance follows a
Student-t distribution, which is defined by three parameters: shape
($\nu=7.8$) , mean ($\mu=0$) and scale ($\sigma= \sigma_j$). By imposing
a variance structure with location (*j*) as the variance covariate,
scale ($\sigma_j$) becomes a function of parameters $\eta$ and $u_j$,
where $e^{\eta}$ represents population-level variability, and $e^{u_j}$
represents deviation of location *j* from the population-level
variability. Finally, $u_j$ is normally distributed, with mean equal to
0 and standard deviation equal to $\sigma_0$.

Density plots for the 4000 sets of parameter estimates generated by the
Bayesian model are provided in the left half of Figs. 4.10 and 4.11. The
peaks of a density plot show where the most likely values (along the
x-axis) of a given parameter are concentrated, similar to a histogram.
They also indicate how much variability exists around parameter
estimates, shown by the shape of the curve (low and broad equals lots of
variability; tall and narrow equals little variability). The y-axis on
density plots represents the probability density function for the kernel
density estimation, and can be disregarded for our purposes. Traces
(right half of Figs. 4.10 and 4.11) indicate how well the parameter
space was sampled in the four chains generated by the NUTS sampler (no
U-turn sampling - an extension of Hamilton Monte Carlo) used when
fitting brms models. Each chain generated 1000 sets of parameter
estimates, for a total of 4000 sets of parameter estimates. For copper,
the traces indicate that the sampling algorithm did not get stuck in one
region of the parameter space, and that the parameter space was well
sampled.

![](images/Bayesian%20Copper_posterior%20densities%201.bmp)

**Figure 4.10** Posterior densities (left) and traces (right) for
parameters associated with fixed effects, obtained from the best-fit
Bayesian model for total copper. In the plots, b_intercept corresponds
to $\beta_0$, b_rain corresponds to $\beta_1$, b_summer1 corresponds to
$\beta_2$, b_sqrt_traffic corresponds to $\beta_3$, and b_devAge2
corresponds to $\beta_4$.

![](images/Bayesian%20Copper_posterior%20densities%202.bmp)

**Figure 4.11** Posterior densities (left) and traces (right) for
parameters associated with random effects, obtained from the best-fit
Bayesian model for total copper. Here, b_sigma_intercept represents
$\eta$ from the random effects equations, sd_agency\_\_Intercept
represents $\sigma_{agency}$, sd_agency:location\_\_Intercept represents
$\sigma_{location}$, sd_location\_\_sigma_Intercept represents
$\sigma_0$, and nu is the Greek letter $\nu$, representing shape of the
Student-t distribution.

Fit of the Bayesian copper model to data can be assessed through RMSE
(0.490) or RSR (0.506), or visualized in estimated versus observed plots
(Figs. 4.12 and 4.13). We provide RSR as a measure of model precision,
since RSR is a standardized form of RMSE. Singh et al. (2004) recommends
that an RSR ≤ 0.50 indicates a well suited model, while Moriasi et al.
(2007) elaborates on this recommendation, suggesting that an RSR ≤ 0.50
indicates a very good model, an RSR ≤ 0.60 indicates a good model, an
RSR ≤ 0.70 indicates a satisfactory model, and RSR \> 0.7 indicates an
unsatisfactory model. According to these guidelines, the copper model
(RSR=0.506) is a good model.

In plots 4.12 and 4.13, the estimated *ln*(copper) values (vertical
axis) are generated using the *fitted* function (brms package; Buerkner
2017), which applies the spatial predictors associated with each data
point (location, rain, summer, sqrt_traffic, devAge2) to all 4000
parameter sets that make up the Bayesian posterior. Mean estimated
values, along with 95% quantiles, are then plotted against observed
*ln*(copper) data (horizontal axis). Ideally, the points should form a
swath along the 1:1 diagonal dashed line. This 1:1 line shows where
estimated values exactly match the observed data. For copper, the
estimated vs. observed plots show slightly better model fit at higher
copper concentrations (Fig. 4.12), evident because points in the upper
right quadrant are closer to the 1:1 line than points in the lower left
quadrant. Within-location variability in the upper right quadrant of
Figure 4.12 is lower than for the lower left quadrant. Locations with
higher copper concentrations also have medium to high values of
sqrt_traffic and high values of devAge2 (Fig. 4.13, top panels). This
could be coincidental, or could be the result of high temporal
variability in copper-contributing sources (e.g., traffic) in
low-traffic locations.

Summer and rain do not display a consistent effect on the Bayesian
model's fit to observed data (Fig. 4.13, bottom panels).

![](images/Bayesian%20Copper_obs%20vs%20est%201.bmp)

**Figure 4.12** Estimated vs. observed plot for the Bayesian copper
model, with point color corresponding to location. Individual points
show how the observed value for *ln*(copper) (horizontal axis) compares
to the mean estimated value from the Bayesian model (vertical axis).
Thin gray vertical lines associated with each point provide the 95%
quantiles for each estimate. Note that residual error is excluded from
the estimates, resulting in narrower 95% quantiles. The diagonal dashed
line shows the 1:1 relationship, where estimated=observed.

![](images/Bayesian%20Copper_obs%20vs%20est%202.bmp)

**Figure 4.13** Estimated vs. observed plots for the Bayesian copper
model, with colors showing the magnitude of one spatial predictor
(sqrt_traffic, devAge2, rain or summer) at each data point. Individual
points show how the observed value for *ln*(copper) compares to the mean
estimated value from the Bayesian model. Diagonal dashed lines show the
1:1 relationship, where estimated=observed.

Copper concentration estimates rely on two spatial predictors:
sqrt_traffic and devAge2, along with two spatio-temporal predictors:
precipitation and season. We can visualize the effect of one spatial
landscape predictor at a time on expected copper concentrations (Fig.
4.14). In this figure, expected mean copper concentrations as a function
of traffic *or* development age are presented as colored credible
interval bands, with S8 Data---used in fitting the Bayesian
model---plotted as black points atop the credible intervals. In order to
generate Figure 4.14, we integrated over the range of values in the S8
Data for rainfall, season, and the non-displayed spatial predictor, to
produce 50%, 80% and 95% credible interval bands. For example, the left
half of Figure 4.14 shows expected mean copper concentrations as a
function of traffic, given the observed range of values for development
age, rainfall and season.

It is important to point out that Figure 4.14 is **not** showing the
Stormwater Heatmap credible intervals by sub-basin. Stormwater Heatmap
credible intervals pertain to a specific sub-basin with known levels of
sqrt_traffic and devAge2, thus are expected to be tighter than the ones
shown in Figure 4.14, which integrate over a range of values for the
non-displayed spatial predictor.

Figure 4.14 credible intervals were calculated using the *epred_draws*
function (tidybayes package; Kay, 2022) applied to a simulated dataset
with all combinations of the following predictors:

- 20% of rain & summer combinations randomly sampled from the S8 Data,
  to provide representative scenarios of rain and summer/ not summer
  conditions;

- eight equally-spaced sqrt_traffic values between minimum and maximum
  sqrt_traffic levels observed in the S8 Data;

- eight equally-spaced devAge2 values between the minimum and maximum
  devAge2 levels observed in the S8 Data.

Following computation of credible intervals, spatial predictors were
unstandardized and back-transformed to generate the figure.

As discussed in Step 9 of Model Construction and Selection, credible
intervals account for uncertainty around fixed effect parameters and
around the variance parameters of the groups, but do not account for
residual variance. This allows stormwater managers to assess the
following:

- What is the likely range for mean copper at a heretofore unsampled
  watershed with a particular level of traffic (or development age)?

This is in line with stormwater management best practices, which manage
for the over-annual impact on water bodies rather than for extreme
events.

![](images/Bayesian%20Copper_cred%20int%20vs%20raw%20data.bmp)**Figure
4.14** Credible intervals for total copper as a function of raw traffic
(Annual Average Daily Traffic; left plot) and development age (right
plot). Bands of color represent 50%, 80% and 95% credible intervals,
while black points represent S8 Data that were used in fitting the
Bayesian model. Expected copper concentrations as a function of traffic
(left plot) integrate over rainfall, season, and development age.
Expected copper concentrations as a function of development age (right
plot) integrate over rainfall, season and traffic.

The Bayesian copper model has a population-level intercept
$\beta_0=2.33$. As a random-intercept model, the location-specific
intercept is allowed to vary by reporting agency (*k*), and by catchment
location within each reporting agency (*j*\|*k*), and sums to:
$\beta_0 + a_k + a_{j|k}$. Density plots for the location-specific
intercept parameters are shown in Figure 4.15, along with the mean and
95% credible intervals for the population-level intercept. Seven of the
14 catchments have location-specific intercepts that overlap well with
the population-level intercept: the majority of their density plots are
shaded blue (see e.g., TAC_COM). Four additional catchments have
approximately half of their density plot overlapping with that of the
population-level intercept (see e.g., TAC_IND). The remaining three
catchments have location-specific intercepts that are quite different
from that of the population (see TAC_HDR, SNO_COM, SEA_IND). The
deviation between location-specific intercepts and the population-level
intercept gives some insight into how much variability may exist in
y-intercept values at unsampled locations. Variability around the
population-level intercept and around group-specific random effects
(reporting agency and location) is captured in the credible intervals
shown in Figure 4.14, as well as in sub-basin credible intervals
presented on the Stormwater Heatmap. Implementing more monitoring across
diverse watershed types would be beneficial to providing more precise
COC estimates and credible intervals.

The Stormwater Heatmap utilizes only the population-level intercept to
estimate mean copper concentrations at unsampled locations; Figure 4.15
is provided as a visual for how much variability exists between
locations, in terms of location-specific intercept.

![](images/Bayesian%20Copper_intercepts.bmp)

**Figure 4.15** Density plots for the 14 location-specific intercept
parameters, along with the median (thick vertical line) and 95% credible
intervals (dashed vertical lines) for the population-level intercept.
For each location, the mean intercept value is indicated with a black
dot, and credible intervals are shown with thick (50% CI) and thin (95%
CI) black horizontal lines. Density plots for each location are shaded
blue for values that fall within the 95% CI for the population-level
intercept, and gray for values that fall outside of the 95% CI for
population-level intercept. Note that the population-level 95% CI does
not incorporate variability around reporting agency $\sigma_{agency}$,
or around location within each reporting agency $\sigma_{location}$; it
is solely the 95% CI for the population-level intercept (i.e.: 95% of
the time, the population-level intercept will fall between the given CI
values).

In summary, the Stormwater Heatmap utilizes the spatial predictors
*sqrt_traffic* and *devAge2* to estimate the over-annual mean copper
concentration. The equation used for visualizing the total copper layer
is:

$$\ln(Cu) = 2.33 + 0.43*sqrt\_traffic + 0.46*devAge2$$

See Applying Mixed Effects Equations to the Stormwater Heatmap at the
end of this document for more information on how the Bayesian model is
simplified to this equation.

The precipitation predictor used for TSS was 1-day cumulative
precipitation. There was no evidence of seasonal patterns to TSS in

Residuals plotted against fitted values showed signs of slight
heterogeneity (Fig 4.17, top left plot). Of the variance structures

$$sd(\epsilon_{ijk}) = \sigma_j $$

The best model for TSS is a random-intercept model, where the intercept
of the linear model is allowed to vary by reporting agency (*k*), and by

or spatial auto-correlation were detected in auto-correlation plots or

Two possible models emerged to capture the fixed effects:

$$ln(TSS_{ijk}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 * rain_i + \beta_2 * sqrt\_traffic_{ijk} + \beta_3 * devAge2_{ijk} + a_k + a_{j|k} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

$$ln(TSS_{ijk}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 * rain_i + \beta_2 * sqrt\_CO_2\_road_{ijk} + \beta_3 * devAge2_{ijk} + a_k + a_{j|k} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$
