## Model Validation with External Data

We performed model validation using nine independent data sets
("validation data") to determine whether the model results are
representative of locations outside of the 14 catchments used to fit and
calibrate the models. This is an important step for ensuring that our
chemical of concern models can be applied to areas across the Puget
Sound region.

The validation process involved several steps:

### Step 1: Identify suitable data

We searched for projects where data were collected in a similar way to
the S8 data used for model fitting. The S8 data were collected from
stormwater outfalls as flow-composite samples during storms with
predicted cumulative rainfall equal to or exceeding 0.25 inches. Ideal
validation data would share these sample characteristics. Because of the
low number of suitable studies with flow-composite samples, we also
included outfalls with grab samples that were collected on three or more
occasions over time. Initially, we treated the grab sampled outfalls
differently in the model validation process, as variability around grab
sample results can be substantially higher than variability around
composite samples. However, as we did not see evidence of higher
variability in the grab-sampled catchments that we had identified, we
ultimately combined grab-sampled outfalls with those sampled using
flow-composite methodology.

### Step 2: Prepare spatial predictors for validation catchments

We obtained or traced spatial polygons for each validation catchments.
Using these polygons, we convolved then calculated the mean spatial
predictor values for each validation catchment.

Convolved mean spatial predictor values for each catchment were
standardized using the spatial predictor means and standard deviations
from the S8 fitting dataset. Standardized spatial predictors were capped
at +/- 2 to prevent extrapolation of model equations beyond the extent
of the fitting data.

### Step 3: Prepare the validation data

We removed validation data that were collected on days when the Daymet
daily surface weather dataset (Thornton et al, 2022) estimated
cumulative daily rainfall at 0mm.

We also used Cleaveland dotplots of the ln-transformed stormwater
validation data to identify and remove outliers. Two high outliers were
removed for zinc (both at OF235), one high outlier was removed for TKN
(at SR9-MP17.92), one high outlier (at SS4) and two low outliers were
removed for TSS (one at OF235, one at OF237A), and one high outlier was
removed for phosphorus (at SR9-MP17.92). The two low outliers for TSS
occurred on days with very low rainfall (Daymet precipitation \< 1mm).

### Step 4: Obtain prediction intervals and fitted values for validation catchments

Using the posterior_predict and fitted function in the brms package
(Buerkner, 2017), we applied the Bayesian water quality models to the
spatio-temporal predictors (landscape predictors, season, Daymet
cumulative rainfall) from the validation catchments to obtain prediction
intervals and fitted values. Prediction intervals predict in what range
a future individual observation will fall. With the nested model
structure for random effects (location nested within agency), prediction
intervals are able to make predictions about future samples both for
known agencies and unknown (new) agencies. This makes them ideal for
comparison to validation data. In the case of the Tacoma S8C validation
dataset, these data were collected by a known agency with an
agency-specific intercept (City of Tacoma), so the prediction intervals
are tighter for Tacoma S8C validation data than for validation data from
unknown agencies.

Fitted values provide a direct comparison between individual samples
collected from validation catchments and model estimates for that
location and weather conditions (rainfall, season).

### Step 5: Compare validation data to model predictions

We plotted the validation data against prediction intervals and fitted
values to visually assess whether validation data fall within a margin
of the model predictions. The following tools were used for visual
assessment:

- Graphical evaluation of validation data plotted atop prediction
  interval bands. We were looking to see if validation data generally
  fit within the 50%, 80% or 95% prediction intervals. This would allow
  us to conclude that the model is representative of the Puget Sound
  basin.

- Graphical evaluation of validation data plotted against model
  predictions (observed versus estimated plots). We were looking for
  validation data to fall relatively close to the 1:1 observed vs.
  estimated line.

- Graphical observation of explanatory reasons for divergence between
  model predictions and validation data.

### Validation Datasets

All validation data were collected between 2004 and 2018. Five composite
data sets and four grab sample data sets were utilized for model
validation, for a total of 28 catchments (Table 4.7). The sampled
catchments span a relatively wide range of the Puget Sound region, with
different land use characteristics (Fig. 4.63). Twenty catchments are
located in urban areas, while eight are located in medium- to
low-density residential areas outside of the Seattle-Tacoma urban
corridor. Of the twenty urban catchments, nine are on high-use roadways
(MLK Street Sweeping project, Washington State DOT project). Three of
the catchments also appear in the S8 fitting data (OF235, OF237B and
OF245), and were resampled by the city of Tacoma for their S8C study.

**Table 4.7.** Sample locations for validation data, including sample
type (composite or grab), location description, and whether the samples
were tested for COCs of interest (Cu=total copper, Zn=total zinc,
TSS=total suspended solids, P=total phosphorus, TKN=total Kjeldahl
nitrogen).

![](images/Table%204_7-01.bmp)

![](images/model%20validation%20comp%20and%20grab%20outfall%20locations.bmp)**Figure
4.63** Locations of test data outfalls used in model validation. Garden
Ed and Lahti Drive outfalls are proximally located and are combined into
one point on the map.

### Validation Catchments - Spatial Predictors

One way of assessing the similarity of the model validation catchments
to the S8 model fitting catchments is to compare the standardized
spatial predictor values for the fitting vs validation catchments.
Standardized spatial predictor values for the validation catchments were
similar to those of the fitting catchments for sqrt_CO2_road, devAge2
and not_greenBE. All of these range roughly between +/-2 (Fig. 4.64). In
contrast, the sqrt_traffic predictor is substantially higher than this
range for a number of the validation catchments (Fig. 4.64). The S8
fitting data did not have any purely roadway catchments, whereas nine of
the validation catchments (those from the MLK Street Sweeping and WA
State DOT projects) are paved roadway with high levels of traffic.

![](images/model%20validation%20predictor%20values.bmp)**Figure 4.64**
Standardized spatial predictor values for sqrt_CO2_road, (purple)
sqrt_traffic (red), devAge2 (orange) and not_greenBE (navy) at the
validation catchments. Dashed lines at y=-2 and y=2 show the values at
which predictors were capped.

As discussed above in "Step 2: Prepare spatial predictors for validation
catchments", all standardized spatial predictors for the validation
catchments were capped at +/- 2 to keep model predictions within the
range represented by the fitting data. Based on the validation results,
this capping value appears appropriate — predictions of stormwater
contaminants from fully-paved, high-traffic catchments would be too high
if the traffic predictor was not capped. It is possible that the
sqrt_traffic predictor is only linear over a certain range of traffic
values, and that the relationship between chemical concentration and
sqrt_traffic levels becomes nonlinear at traffic values outside of those
seen in the S8 fitting data.

### Validation Results

#### Total Copper

Six of the nine model validation projects (22 catchments total) analyzed
stormwater samples for total copper. These copper data are plotted atop
prediction intervals for their catchments (Fig. 4.65). Prediction
intervals show the range into which future samples might fall. In
general, our copper model tended to over-estimate copper concentrations
in the validation catchments, with the exception of several highway
sites (catchments beginning with I5) and the sites in Coupeville
(BoatLaunch, CoupevilleWharf, FrontAndMain): the majority of samples
from these catchments fell within the 50% prediction intervals.

Tacoma S8C outfalls (samples beginning with OF) have somewhat narrower
prediction intervals because the agency (the random effect) has a known
agency-specific intercept from the model fitting process.

![](images/model%20validation_Copper%20prediction%20boxplot.bmp)

**Figure 4.65** Box and whisker plots for copper validation data, shown
atop model-generated prediction intervals. Dark orange bands represent
the 50% prediction intervals, where 50% of future data points would be
expected to lie, light orange bands represent 80% prediction intervals,
and peach bands represent 95% prediction intervals.

Estimated vs. observed plots show the model estimated values for each
catchment plotted against observed validation data (Fig. 4.66, 4.67 and
4.68). Figure 4.66 shows all observed data points and their model
estimated values. Figure 4.67 shows a series of estimated vs. observed
plots where colors indicate the spatio-temporal predictor values
associated with each catchment and sample. Lastly, Figure 4.68 shows the
median estimated value vs. the median observed value as a summary of the
data for each catchment. Ideally, data points should lie close to the
1:1 line indicating that model estimates are close to the observed
values. For copper, many data points have higher estimated values than
the actual observed values.

Several samples from the Tacoma outfalls (OF235, OF237A, OF243) had
estimated values substantially higher than their observed values (see
upper left, Fig. 4.66). These samples were collected in the summer
during very low rainfall events (Fig. 4.67, bottom panels). Two
explanations exist for this overestimation. It is possible that the rain
and summer coefficients in our copper model are not suitably addressing
low rainfall/ summer conditions. It is also possible that the level of
rainfall was too low to convey copper particles to the stormwater
outfall, resulting in less polluted water entering the outfall during
these sampling events.

#### Total Suspended Solids

Seven of the nine model validation projects (25 catchments total)
analyzed stormwater samples for total suspended solids. These TSS data
are plotted atop prediction intervals for their catchments (Fig. 4.69).
Prediction intervals show the range into which future samples might
fall. In general, the 50% prediction intervals (dark orange, Fig. 4.69)
overlap well with validation data. For most catchments, the 95%
prediction intervals extend far beyond the range of the data points,
indicating that the S8 fitting data may have had higher variability
around TSS data points than the validation data.

Tacoma S8C outfalls (samples beginning with OF) have somewhat narrower
prediction intervals because the agency (the random effect) has a known
agency-specific intercept from the model fitting process.

![](images/model%20validation_TSS%20prediction%20boxplot-01.bmp)**Figure
4.69** Box and whisker plots for TSS validation data, shown atop
model-generated prediction intervals. Dark orange bands represent the
50% prediction intervals, where 50% of future data points would be
expected to lie, light orange bands represent 80% prediction intervals,
and peach bands represent 95% prediction intervals.

Estimated vs. observed plots show the model estimated values for each
catchment plotted against observed validation data (Fig. 4.70, 4.71 and
4.72). Figure 4.70 shows all observed data points and their model
estimated values. Figure 4.71 shows a series of estimated vs. observed
plots where colors indicate the spatio-temporal predictor values
associated with each catchment and sample. Lastly, Figure 4.72 shows the
median estimated value vs. the median observed value as a summary of the
data for each catchment. Ideally, data points should lie close to the
1:1 line indicating that model estimates are close to the observed
values. For TSS, the validation data points are arranged in a cloud
centered around the 1:1 line (Fig. 4.70). Figure 4.72 shows that our
model is overestimating TSS values for five outfalls from two agencies
(KIR-CW, N.MER, REN-JC, HS-033, NB-020).

The subplots in Figure 4.71 do not indicate a strong pattern of
correlation between data points farther from the 1:1 line and magnitude
of the spatio-temporal predictors. The rainfall plot (Fig. 4.71, lower
left) indicates a possible correlation between low 1-day cumulative
rainfall and greater distance between data points and the 1:1 line.

## Model Fitting Conclusions

Summary by COC of how confident we are in our models

- how did the model fitting go overall?

- how did the sensitivity analysis go? any concerns there?

- how well does the validation data corroborate the model that was
  selected?

- are there COCs where additional data would be helpful (for fitting? Or
  for validation?)

- anything readers/ users of the SWHM should be aware of for each COC?

#### Total Copper

The spatial predictor model for total copper is a clear improvement over
the land use category model, and has good fit to the S8 fitting data.
The spatial predictor model has an AIC value nearly four points lower
than that of the categorical land use model as assessed in the
frequentist model fitting. Furthermore, error bars around the spatial
predictor model covariates were much smaller than error bars around
covariates from the land use category model (Fig.4.9).

During the Bayesian model fitting steps, we noted that the spatial
predictor model fits well to data from high sqrt_traffic and high devAge
2 (old development) outfalls (Fig. 4.13). The model seems to over- or
under-predict total copper in some of the low-traffic outfalls from the
S8 dataset. Additionally, location-specific intercepts arising from the
nested structure of the model showed some variability between sites
(Fig. 4.15). This indicates that we might expect total copper levels to
vary somewhat from our model predictions in new locations, although the
slope of the relationship between ln(Cu) and scaled and centered
sqrt_traffic or devAge2 should be consistent.

The spatial predictor model for total copper fits the S8 data well and
is robust to changes in the model structure. The calculated RSR for the
Bayesian total copper model is 0.506, indicating a model on the cusp of
good and very good. Removing influential data points (only 2 for copper)
or changing the variance structure resulted in \<1% change to model
coefficients. Removing the nesting structure from the model had a larger
but not dramatic effect on model coefficients (8% change in sqrt_traffic
coefficient, 3% change in devAge2 coefficient).

Model validation was performed using copper data from 22 outfalls that
included busy streets, highway areas, high-density urban or industrial
areas, and lower density residential areas. The total copper model
generally fits the trends of the validation locations well: areas with
high traffic or old development are correctly predicted to have higher
copper concentrations than areas with low traffic and/or new/low
development (Fig.4.65). However, the model generally over-predicts the
range of possible copper values for most outfalls (Fig. 4.65). The model
fit data from high traffic locations very well (Fig. 4.67), but
over-predicted copper for other areas. Low rainfall frequently coincided
with data points that fell outside of the model predictions (Fig. 4.67).

In general, we think the copper model is a solid improvement over land
use category models, and can be relied upon to show areas that are
likely to have higher magnitudes of total copper in stormwater
throughout the Puget Sound Basin. The overall estimates (especially 80
and 95% prediction intervals) may be higher than reality, particularly
for low traffic/ newer development watersheds.

#### Total Suspended Solids

The spatial predictor model for TSS is a clear improvement over the land
use category model, and has good fit to the S8 fitting data. The spatial
predictor model has an AIC value six and a half points lower than that
of the categorical land use model as assessed in the frequentist model
fitting. Furthermore, error bars around the spatial predictor model
covariates were much smaller than error bars around covariates from the
land use category model (Fig.4.20).

In the Bayesian model fitting plots, we see a large spread in TSS values
at each location (e.g., Fig. 4.23). The rainfall predictor for TSS is
1-day rainfall, while all other COC models have a 14- to 21-day
cumulative rainfall predictor. It could be that an additional temporal
predictor (season, longer duration cumulative rainfall) might improve
model fit for TSS by accurately capturing within-site variability. (In
the frequentist model fitting steps, we tested summer as a temporal
predictor, but found it to not be significant for TSS.)
Location-specific intercepts arising from the nested structure of the
model showed little variability between sites (Fig. 4.26), indicating
that we might expect the TSS model to fit well at new locations.

The calculated RSR for the Bayesian TSS model is 0.81, indicating an
unsatisfactory model. However, the large spread in TSS values over time
at each location is a clear contributor to the high RSR value. Because
the Stormwater Heatmap links chemicals of concern to *spatial* landscape
predictors (rather than temporal ones), we think that the high RSR is
not reflective of the model's utility in this context.

The TSS model is robust to changes in the model structure. Removing
influential data points (3 for TSS) or changing the variance structure
resulted in a maximum of 3.3% change to model coefficients. Removing the
nesting structure from the model had a moderate effect on the
sqrt_traffic coefficient (10.5% change), but very little effect on the
devAge2 coefficient (1.1% change) and the intercept (0.2% change).

Model validation was performed using TSS data from 25 outfalls that
included busy streets, highway areas, high density urban or industrial
areas, and low density residential areas. The TSS model fits the
validation locations well. The upper bounds of the 95% prediction
intervals are well above the range of the TSS validation data, but the
50% prediction intervals are very good at capturing the median, and 80%
prediction intervals capture almost all outlying data points (Fig.
4.69). As with the S8 fitting data, the validation catchments also show
a broad spread of TSS values over time for each catchment. Low
quantities of rainfall may have limited effectiveness at transporting
solids to storm drains, resulting in high variability over time, or
unexplored seasonal predictors may also have an effect.

In general, we think the TSS model is a solid improvement over land use
category models, and can be relied upon to show locations of high TSS in
the Puget Sound Basin. The model also has been shown to provide reliable
predictions for TSS magnitude at new locations. Large variability in TSS
values at each location may be the result of variable effectiveness of
precipitation in transporting solids to storm drains, or unexplored
seasonal effects, including autumn, winter or spring.

## Translating Equations to the Stormwater Heatmap

The process of translating water quality equations for constituents of
concern to the Stormwater Heatmap involved manipulation of the spatial
predictor data grid followed by application of Bayesian COC equations to
calculate estimated COC concentrations by location.

### Preparing Spatial Predictors Images Across the Puget Sound Basin

Multi-band spatial landscape predictor images across the Puget Sound
basin (described in Chapter 2: High-Resolution Land Cover) were first
transformed (traffic and CO2_road predictors were square-root
transformed, and devAge was squared) then scaled and centered using the
mean and standard deviation from the fourteen S8 catchment locations.
The resulting images were convolved with a circular kernel of 100 meters
to calculate the mean value in the neighborhood of each point. Finally,
the convolved spatial predictor images were clamped at +/- 2 standard
deviations of the S8 catchment location values. Clamping was necessary
to avoid extrapolating beyond the range where linear relationships
between spatial predictors and COCs may no longer apply. Figure 4.66
shows the range of predictor values for the S8 catchments, along with
the minimum and maximum predictor values across the Puget Sound basin,
while Figure 4.67 shows histograms of observed spatial predictor values
across the Puget Sound.

![](images/spatial%20predictor%20values%20in%20S8%20data%20and%20in%20Puget%20Sound%20Basin_temp.bmp)**Figure
4.66** Plot showing the range of scaled and centered values for each
spatial predictor found in the S8 Data (orange bar and black data
points), along with the extent of values found within the Puget Sound
basin (gray lines). The magenta bars extend the orange bars to the
values at which spatial predictors were clamped. Note that the upper
extent of the grey line for sqrt_traffic should be at 62, but has been
truncated to provide an appropriate scale for the other predictors.

![](images/spatial%20predictor%20distribution_Puget%20Sound%20basin.bmp)

**Figure 4.67** Histogram of scaled and centered spatial predictor
values for the Puget Sound basin. The y-axis in all plots shows the
square-root transformed number of observations for each scaled and
centered spatial predictor value.

Clamping the traffic predictor was especially important because traffic
levels on high-volume roads such as freeways can far exceed the traffic
levels in our monitored catchments. The maximum raw traffic value was
clamped at 5,000 AADT, whereas on highways in the Puget Sound basin (not
analyzed in this study) traffic can reach 100,000 AADT.

Based on highway runoff data from the whole United States (USGS Highway
Runoff DataBase, accessed 11/01/21), we observed that linear equations
relating TSS to traffic volume provides estimates that are too high when
traffic is allowed to reach levels near 240,000. When traffic volumes
are clamped at 31,000 ADT, the estimates are more believable. This
suggests that, for at least some COCs, traffic may be a linear predictor
at the traffic volumes in the S8 catchments, but may reach an asymptote
at high traffic volumes. It also suggests that caution should be used
when interpreting estimates for areas with exceptionally high traffic
volumes.

### Preparing Visualization Layers

To visualize COC concentrations via a webmap, we applied water quality
regression equations to the prepared spatial predictor images to
generate predicted concentrations for the study area.

Using the scaled and centered multi-band spatial landscape predictor
image, we employed the following steps to generate heatmap layers.

Regression equations were applied to the convolved spatial predictor
dataset (regression equations were applied using spatial predictor
values in each grid box.)

### Applying Mixed Effects Equations to the Stormwater Heatmap

The equations that were fitted to the S8 monitoring data required a
specified variance structure to account for heteroskedasticity, as well
as a nested structure for the random effects. Homoskedasticity is an
important pre-requisite to constructing linear models between predictors
and dependent variables, and both the locations and the agencies had
some level of variability in the spreads of their data (Fig. 4.68).

![](images/TSS%20variability%20by%20location%20and%20agency_color.bmp)**Figure
4.68** Spread of the S8 monitoring data for total suspended solids (TSS)
by location (top) and by reporting agency (bottom), with color coding by
reporting agency. Note the variability in spread per location (e.g.,
blue boxes vs. green boxes) as well as per reporting agency (e.g., red
boxes vs. green boxes).

With respect to translating mixed effects model equations to the
Stormwater Heatmap, the equations are substantially simplified.
Predicting mean COC concentrations allow the variance structure and
nested random effects terms to go to their mean values of 0.
Furthermore, rainfall and the summer predictor, where applicable, are
also set to their mean value of 0. Thus the generic COC equation:
$$\ln(COC_{ijk}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1*rain_i + \beta_2*summer_i + \beta_3*predictor1_{ijk} + \beta_4*predictor2_{ijk} + a_k + a_{j|k} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

$$a_k \sim N(0, \sigma_{agency})$$

$$a_{j|k}\sim N(0, \sigma_{location})$$

$$\epsilon_{ijk} \sim N(0, \sigma_k)$$

becomes simplified to:

$$\ln(COC) = \beta_0 + \beta_1*0 + \beta_2*0 + \beta_3*predictor1 + \beta_4
*predictor2 + 0 + 0 + 0$$

and finally:

$$\ln(COC) = \beta_0 + \beta_3*predictor1 + \beta_4*predictor2$$
